analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license to own handguns and semi-automatic rifles and records every sale.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on June 30, 2026, with one cosponsor, and was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has had no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The Blair Holt Act would make it a federal crime, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, to possess a handgun or a semi-automatic rifle with a detachable magazine holding more than 10 rounds unless you have a federal firearm owner license. To get a license you would submit a photograph, fingerprints, and personal history to the Attorney General, pass a criminal background check, and pay a fee capped at $10; existing owners would have two years to comply. Every sale or transfer of these guns would have to go through a licensed dealer, who would verify the buyer's license and file a report with the manufacturer, model, and serial number into a new federal record of sale system. The bill also requires reporting lost or stolen guns within 72 hours, creates penalties when a child gets access to an unsecured gun and someone is hurt, and funds federal research on gun injuries.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the main beneficiaries would be people exposed to gun violence — the bill's own findings cite roughly 44,000 gun deaths in 2024 and note that Black children and teens are 16 times more likely than White children to die from gun violence. Licensing is designed to keep guns away from people prohibited from having them and to require owners to demonstrate safe handling; the record of sale system is designed to let police trace crime guns. People who already own these firearms can keep them if they get licensed, and hunting, range use, and family gift transfers get specific exemptions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities hit hardest by gun violence

how_it_helps.text: It would make it unlawful for anyone without a federal or state firearm owner license to possess a handgun or a semi-automatic rifle that accepts a detachable magazine holding more than 10 rounds, with licensing requiring fingerprinting, a background check, and basic eligibility screening.

Every sale or transfer of one of these firearms would have to go through a licensed dealer, who would verify the buyer's license and file a report identifying the firearm and the parties — creating a record of sale that law enforcement can use to trace guns used in crimes.

Owners would have to report lost or stolen firearms within 72 hours, notify the Attorney General of address changes, and could face penalties if a child gains access to an unsecured gun and someone is killed or seriously hurt.

It would establish a federal firearm injury clearinghouse and direct the Attorney General to study the causes of gun deaths and injuries, including research on smart-gun technology, ending a period in which such federal research has been minimal.

analysis.who_pays: If it passed, the cost would fall on tens of millions of current and future handgun and semi-automatic rifle owners, who would need to apply, be fingerprinted, and renew a license every five years to keep guns they may already own, with up to 10 years in prison for possessing one unlicensed. Most private transfers outside immediate family would require a dealer. The firearms industry would face new recordkeeping, reporting, and inspection duties, and dealers would have to process every private sale.
analysis.who_pays_short: Handgun and rifle owners; gun industry

drawbacks.text: The bill makes it a crime punishable by up to 10 years in prison to possess a handgun or semi-automatic rifle without a license, meaning otherwise law-abiding owners who miss the compliance deadline face felony exposure.

The bill strikes the existing federal prohibition on establishing a firearms registration system and requires dealers to file reports identifying the manufacturer, model, and serial number of every transferred qualifying firearm into a federal record of sale system — a registry of transactions that gun owners and gun rights organizations have long opposed.

Applicants must authorize release of their mental health records to the Attorney General and certify details about past treatment, raising privacy concerns; and private transfers outside a narrow list of family relationships must go through a licensed dealer, adding cost and friction for ordinary buyers and sellers.

Most Americans who already own handguns or semi-automatic rifles would need to obtain a license within two years of enactment, with fingerprinting, a photograph, and a background check for a right many currently exercise without federal permission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit is real: licensing and traceable sale records are the mechanisms that make it harder for prohibited, untrained, or straw-purchasing buyers to get handguns, and they give police a way to trace crime guns — aims the bill's findings tie to roughly 44,000 gun deaths a year, falling hardest on communities of color. The costs are also real and fall on ordinary people, not just industry: tens of millions of existing handgun and semi-automatic rifle owners would have to be photographed, fingerprinted, and licensed, with up to 10 years in prison for failing to comply; most private transfers between people outside the immediate family would require going through a dealer; and a federal record of sale holding serial-number-level data would replace the current federal ban on building a registration system. Whether that trade is worth it is a genuine policy judgment, but the bill as written asks a large compliance burden from all gun owners to reach a narrower population of misuse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearings, no votes, and no movement.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on June 30, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
No further action has been taken since the referral — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote.
The bill has a single cosponsor, meaning it entered the House with essentially no visible support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: As of now, no one has won or lost — the bill has not advanced, so current federal gun law remains unchanged, and neither gun owners nor communities affected by gun violence have seen anything happen.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; current gun law unchanged

for.name: Rep. Jonathan L. Jackson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 30, 2026, naming it for Blair Holt, a Chicago teenager killed shielding a classmate on a school bus in 2007.

for.name: Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's sole cosponsor at introduction.

sides.party_line_note: No vote has occurred, so no partisan split is recorded; both sponsors are Democrats, and no Republican has signed on.

industries.note: Licensing and a record of sale for every handgun and semi-automatic rifle transaction adds compliance requirements and could shrink the pool of eligible buyers, cutting into sales of the most popular firearm categories. Manufacturers also face federal collection of production and sales figures and inspections.

The bill channels every private sale through a licensed dealer, which creates mandated business, but dealers also absorb the recordkeeping, verification, and inspection obligations, with criminal penalties for failures.

analysis.trajectory: With two sponsors, no committee action since referral, and only months left in the 119th Congress, the bill is likely to die in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote — the same fate as earlier versions of this measure introduced repeatedly over the past two decades.
